newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen higher at open.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen higher at open.

text.p: A couple of huge mergers could catapult the market into higher ground to kickoff the holiday-shortened week.

The mergers are expected to spread interest to the overall market and perhaps help the Dow Jones industrial average climb back above the 7,000 mark, which it reached last Thursday before settling back on Friday.
"Mergers are supportive of the market. They build momentum as investors search out other opportunities," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Marriott International Inc said it had agreed to acquire Renaissance Hotel Group N.V for $30 cash per share in a transaction valued at $1 billion, including transaction costs and assumption of Renaissance debt.
H.F. Ahmanson and Co said it had offered to acquire Great Western Financial Corp in a stock swap valued at $6 billion.
Healthsouth Corp and Horizon/CMS Healthcare Corp said they have definitively agreed to merge in a stock pact valued at about $1.6 billion, including the assumption of about $700 million in debt.
"We are seeing a consolidation of companies which will mean stronger financial entities," Cardillo said.
Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities, said that the broader story remained the flow of money into index mutual funds which buy blue chip stocks and push the averages higher.
"This money get placed immediately in the S&P 500 stocks which push the S&P and Dow indexes higher," Wachtel said.

Analysts said that shares of companies such as AT&T Corp could get a boost from a deal to bring free-trade principals to the telecom industry, clinched under the auspicies of the World Trade Organization in Geneva Saturday.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average fell 279.90 points, or 1.49 percent, to the day's low of 18,470.75.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 1.7 at 4339.5
Among U.S. shares traded in London, Philip Morris Cos Inc rose to 127-1/4, up 1-3/4 from its New York close Friday.
The dollar was firm but off its highs in Tokyo and edged lower in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly higher, with the long bond up 5/32 to yield 6.52 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Wall Street investors, having lost hundreds of millions of dollars as Ronald Perelman dragged Marvel Entertainment Group Inc into bankruptcy court, now are rejoicing over every small setback for the New York millionare.

The New York Times Market Place writes that according to a new study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, younger mutual fund managers can earn much higher returns than old managers. Their study concluded that the younger the manager, the better the performance.
